entry.gloss: scale type set by its step pattern and home note
entry.def: A type of scale defined by its pattern of whole and half steps and the note it treats as home. The seven diatonic modes each use the pattern of the major scale starting from a different degree: on the white keys of the piano, Ionian runs from C to C, Dorian from D to D, and so on up to Locrian from B. Major and minor are themselves modes.

entry.gloss: the modes of medieval and Renaissance chant and polyphony
entry.def: The modes of medieval and Renaissance music: originally eight, the Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian and Mixolydian modes, each in an authentic form and a plagal (hypo-) form whose range lies a fourth lower. In 1547 Heinrich Glarean added the Aeolian and Ionian modes, making twelve; the Locrian mode remained theoretical. Also called ecclesiastical modes.

entry.gloss: home note of a mode, where melodies end
entry.def: The note on which a melody in a mode normally ends, its equivalent of a tonic: D for the Dorian mode, E for Phrygian, F for Lydian and G for Mixolydian. From the Latin finalis.

entry.gloss: the note that sets a mode apart from major or minor
entry.def: The note that distinguishes a mode from the major or natural minor scale on the same tonic: the raised sixth of Dorian, the lowered second of Phrygian, the raised fourth of Lydian, the lowered seventh of Mixolydian and the lowered fifth of Locrian. Also called the characteristic tone or color note.

figure.caption: C Lydian: a C major scale with a raised fourth degree.

entry.gloss: mode with the same steps as the major scale
entry.def: The mode with the pattern of the major scale: whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half. On the white keys it runs from C to C.

figure.staff: C4 D4 E4 F4 G4 A4 B4 C5

entry.gloss: minor with a raised sixth
entry.def: The mode with the pattern whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half, whole: a natural minor scale with a raised sixth degree. On the white keys it runs from D to D. It is common in folk music and jazz.

figure.staff: D4 E4 F4 G4 A4 *B4{6} C5 D5
figure.caption: D Dorian: D natural minor with B instead of Bb.

entry.gloss: minor with a lowered second
entry.def: The mode with the pattern half, whole, whole, whole, half, whole, whole: a natural minor scale with a lowered second degree, a half step above the tonic. On the white keys it runs from E to E.

figure.staff: E4 *F4{2} G4 A4 B4 C5 D5 E5
figure.caption: E Phrygian: E natural minor with F instead of F#.

entry.gloss: major with a raised fourth
entry.def: The mode with the pattern whole, whole, whole, half, whole, whole, half: a major scale with a raised fourth degree, a tritone above the tonic. On the white keys it runs from F to F.

figure.staff: F4 G4 A4 *B4{4} C5 D5 E5 F5
figure.caption: F Lydian: F major with B instead of Bb.

entry.gloss: major with a lowered seventh
entry.def: The mode with the pattern whole, whole, half, whole, whole, half, whole: a major scale with a lowered seventh degree, a subtonic instead of a leading tone. On the white keys it runs from G to G. It is common in folk and rock music.

figure.staff: G4 A4 B4 C5 D5 E5 *F5{7} G5
figure.caption: G Mixolydian: G major with F instead of F#.

entry.gloss: mode with the same steps as natural minor
entry.def: The mode with the pattern of the natural minor scale: whole, half, whole, whole, half, whole, whole. On the white keys it runs from A to A. Its lowered sixth degree sets it apart from the Dorian mode.

figure.staff: A4 B4 C5 D5 E5 *F5{6} G5 A5

entry.gloss: mode with a lowered second and fifth
entry.def: The mode with the pattern half, whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole: a natural minor scale with lowered second and fifth degrees. On the white keys it runs from B to B. Its tonic triad is diminished, so it was hardly used before the twentieth century.

entry.gloss: moving music to another pitch level
entry.def: Rewriting or performing music at a different pitch, moving every note by the same interval, so that the intervals between the notes stay the same. Transposing to a new key also changes the key signature. Music for transposing instruments is written transposed.

figure.staff: C4/q E4/q G4/q | F4/q E4/q D4/q | C4/h. |.
D4/q F#4/q A4/q | G4/q F#4/q E4/q | D4/h. |.
figure.caption: A melody in C major transposed up a major second to D major.

entry.gloss: instrument that sounds at a different pitch than written
entry.def: An instrument whose music is written at a different pitch from the one it sounds, so that players can use the same fingerings on instruments of different sizes. The key in its name is the note that sounds when it plays a written C: a written C on the clarinet in B♭ sounds Bb.

entry.gloss: the pitch that actually sounds
entry.def: The pitch that is actually heard, as opposed to the written pitch of a transposing instrument; the piano, violin and flute play at concert pitch. The term also names the standard tuning, today usually A4 at 440 vibrations per second.

entry.gloss: the note as it appears in the player's part
entry.def: The note as notated in a player's part. For a transposing instrument it differs from the concert pitch by the instrument's interval of transposition; for other instruments the two are the same.

entry.gloss: score showing each part as its player reads it
entry.def: A score in which the parts of transposing instruments are written as their players read them, at written pitch. Most orchestral scores are transposed.

entry.gloss: score with every part at sounding pitch
entry.def: A score in which every part is written at concert pitch, so that the conductor or analyst reads the sounding notes directly; instruments that sound an octave away may keep their usual octave. Also called a score in C.

entry.gloss: woodwind sounding a major second lower
entry.def: The most common clarinet, which sounds a major second lower than written: a written D5 sounds C5. Its parts are written a major second higher than concert pitch, with two more sharps or two fewer flats in the key signature.

figure.caption: Written notes (upper staff) and the sounding notes (lower staff).

entry.gloss: woodwind sounding a minor third lower
entry.def: A clarinet a half step lower than the clarinet in B♭, which sounds a minor third lower than written: a written C5 sounds A4. Its key signature has three more flats or three fewer sharps than concert pitch, which suits sharp keys.

figure.caption: Written notes (upper staff) and the sounding notes (lower staff).

entry.gloss: brass sounding a major second lower
entry.def: The most common trumpet, which like the clarinet in B♭ sounds a major second lower than written: a written E5 sounds D5. Orchestral players also use trumpets in C, which do not transpose.

figure.caption: Written notes (upper staff) and the sounding notes (lower staff).

entry.gloss: brass sounding a perfect fifth lower
entry.def: The French horn, which sounds a perfect fifth lower than written: a written C5 sounds F4. Modern parts have one more sharp or one fewer flat than concert pitch; older horn parts are written without a key signature. Simply called the horn by players.

figure.caption: Written notes (upper staff) and the sounding notes (lower staff).

entry.gloss: double reed sounding a perfect fifth lower
entry.def: A larger, lower oboe in F, which sounds a perfect fifth lower than written, like the horn in F. Despite its name it is neither English nor a horn. Called the cor anglais in British English.

figure.caption: Written notes (upper staff) and the sounding notes (lower staff).

entry.gloss: saxophone sounding a major sixth lower
entry.def: The saxophone in Eb, which sounds a major sixth lower than written: a written C5 sounds Eb4. Its parts have three more sharps or three fewer flats than concert pitch.

figure.caption: Written notes (upper staff) and the sounding notes (lower staff).

entry.gloss: saxophone sounding a major ninth lower
entry.def: The saxophone in Bb, which sounds a major ninth, an octave and a major second, lower than written: a written D5 sounds C4. Its parts have two more sharps or two fewer flats than concert pitch.

figure.caption: Written notes (upper staff) and the sounding notes (lower staff).

entry.gloss: small flute sounding an octave higher
entry.def: A small flute that sounds an octave higher than written, which keeps its very high notes from needing many ledger lines. The usual English name comes from the Italian flauto piccolo, little flute.

figure.caption: Written notes (upper staff) and the sounding notes (lower staff).

entry.gloss: bowed string sounding an octave lower
entry.def: The largest and lowest instrument of the violin family's section in the orchestra, which sounds an octave lower than written in the bass clef, so that its low notes need fewer ledger lines. Also called the contrabass, string bass or simply bass.

figure.caption: Written notes (upper staff) and the sounding notes (lower staff).

entry.gloss: plucked string sounding an octave lower
entry.def: The six-string guitar, whose music is written in the treble clef an octave higher than it sounds; the clef often has a small 8 below it to show this. Its open strings sound E2, A2, D3, G3, B3 and E4.

figure.staff: E3 A3 D4 G4 B4 E5
figure.caption: The open strings, written in the octave treble clef; they sound an octave lower than the unmarked treble clef would show.
